newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists agree vote strategy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists agree vote strategy.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist and Communist leaders warily agreed a snap election pact on Tuesday that covers job creation and shorter working hours, but avoids a chasm over Europe.

Socialist Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue, whose parties have been uneasy allies when not outright enemies for nearly 80 years, said the left was offering an alternative to austerity by the ruling centre-right in the May 25-June 1 poll.

"The fight against unemployment and for jobs is an absolute priority," the two said in a seven-page declaration whose main policies were drawn from a Socialist platform. "Together, we reject the idea that people be asked to make new sacrifices."

They agreed to revive the economy, create 700,000 youth jobs, raise salaries, cut the working week to 35 hours from 39, reform taxes and halt privatisations of companies including Air France and France Telecom.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe blasted the deal as "demagogic" on public spending, "very backward-looking" on the public sector, "very interventionist" on working hours, "verbose" on Europe and lax on illegal immigration.

Jospin and Hue, noting they were fighting the first round of the election on separate platforms, said the declaration was not a blueprint for a coalition if they upset polls showing Juppe's coalition is likely to retain a majority in parliament.
"We cannot hide our differences," Hue said. Jospin said that the centre-right had merely "a facade of unity".

The statement skirted deep disagreements on European integration. Jospin broadly favours a single European currency, but Hue opposed the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 referendum and wants a new referendum on the euro.
"The respective positions of the Socialist party and the Communist party on Europe are well known," the statement said.
The two nevertheless said they wanted talks between European countries on "redirecting European integration towards a social Europe for progress, peace and security".
"We say no to a liberal Europe, to the Europe where money is king, and to submission to financial markets," it said, adding a "new path" was possible based on a leftist agenda.
Illustrating their divergences, Hue and Jospin gave separate news conferences after their talks in Paris' Latin Quarter.
"We are in favour of monetary union but we don't want a dogmatic reading of the Maastricht treaty," Jospin said, reiterating the Socialists wanted the single currency but only on certain conditions.
Jospin's party is forecast by most opinion polls to win about 220 seats compared with only 25 or so for the Communists in the 577-seat National Assembly.
Jospin reiterated that he was not opposed in principle to Communists taking part in government, but he warned Hue at his news conference that it would have to be on Socialist terms.
"If there is a government of the forces of change, the government will follow only one line. As far as we're concerned, if the French people give us their confidence, it will be ours," Jospin said.

Jospin has had blunt words for the Communists in recent days, telling them they have to review policies after the end of the Cold War, apparently trying to counter warnings by centre-right politicians of a "Red menace".
The French Communist Party was long one of the most staunchly pro-Soviet in Europe, run on strict Stalinist lines.
